vikisozluk.baslik: هَجَا • (hajā) I (non-past يَهْجُو (yahjū), verbal noun هَجْو (hajw) or هِجَاء (hijāʔ))
anlam: to speak poorly of, to satirize, to dispraise or revile with words, to lampoon
to pronounce or speak of something's various traits or flaws
to pronounce syllables, to spell out, to annunciate or make plain the various sounds of a word

vikisozluk.baslik: هَجَّى • (hajjā) II (non-past يُهَجِّي (yuhajjī), verbal noun تَهْجِيَة (tahjiya))
تَهَجَّى • (tahajjā) V (non-past يَتَهَجَّى (yatahajjā), verbal noun تَهَجٍّ (tahajjin))
هَجْوِيّ • (hajwiyy) (feminine هَجْوِيَّة (hajwiyya), masculine plural هَجْوِيُّون (hajwiyyūn), feminine plural هَجْوِيَّات (hajwiyyāt))

etymarab.kok_maddesi: Back to library EtymArab HǦW هجو BP – • HDAL • © SG | 12Mar2026 √HǦW “root” ▪ HǦW_1 ‘to ridicule, mock, satirize, lampoon’ ↗ haǧā ; ‘derision, scoffing, satire; defamatory poem’ ↗¹ hiǧāʔ ▪ HǦW_2 ‘spelling, successive order of letters; alphabet’ ↗² hiǧāʔ Other values, now obsolete, include (Hava1899): ▪ † HǦW_3 ‘to be hot (day)’: † haǧuwa ( u , haǧāwaẗ ) ▪ † HǦW_4 ‘...’: † hǧw ▪ [gnrl] : WehrCowan1976 groups [v1] and [v2] together in one entry, suggesting that they belong to the same root. But others separate the two, a practice followed also here, as a semantic connection between them is not obvious. The same goes for the now obsolete † [v3]. See, however, below, remarks on [v2]. ▪ [v1] : The value ‘to ridicule, mock, satirize, lampoon’ has no cognates in other Sem languages or outside (unless it should have developed from [v2], see below). – DRS remarks the semantic proximity to ↗√HǦL ( † haǧǧala ‘to impair the reputation of s.o., revile s.o. in words)’ 1 and ↗√HǦN (↗ haǧǧana ‘to excoriate, flay, censure scathingly, run down, disparage’, haǧuna ‘to be incorrect or faulty’, huǧnaẗ ‘fault, defect, shortcoming’, haǧīn ‘low, lowly, base, ignoble, mean’, ĭstahǧana ‘to consider bad, wrong or improper; to disapprove of s.th., condemn, reject’, 2 a comparison that seems to make sense. Ar haǧā in the sense of [v1] as well as † haǧǧala and † haǧana may thus be extensions in -W , -L and -N , respectively, all based on a 2-cons. root nucleus signifying s.th. like *‘low, base, to degrade, run down, etc.’. ▪ [v2] : Ar haǧǧà ‘to spell’, ² hiǧāʔ ‘spelling, successive order of letters; alphabet’ and derivatives go back to the idea of ‘splitting up into syllables/sounds’ that is also found in other Sem languages (postBiblHbr, modHbr, TargAram Syr Mnd, often with further development into ‘letter, syllable, syllabification; pronouncing, speech, sound; to vocalise, read, brood over, study’) and with all likelihood has developed, via ‘to recite murmuring’, from a primary ‘murmuring, moaning, sighing, whispering, growling (lion), cooing (pigeon), rumbling (thunder)’ or similar sounds that all imply some kind of “stammering”, interruption or pausing (cf. also the Ug cognate hg ‘to count; counting’ sc. to give the student time to meditate/ponder/muse about the meaning of the text’, then also ‘meditation, study, etc.’ (Hbr, JudAram, Syr, Mnd, Te). Ar hiǧāʔ ‘spelling; alphabet’ is thus akin to, among other items, the interesting Hbr term higgāyōn that originally signifies a ‘pausing’ in reading a psalm, but then also developed into a musical technical term. 3 – If it should turn out, against our assumption, that [v1] ‘to ridicule, mock, satirize, lampoon’ and [v2] ‘to split up in syllables, spell’ are related, then [v2] is prob. the primary value, given the Ug, Hbr and Aram cognates and hence the attestation of a deeper (C)Sem layer. Klein1987 thinks that the Sem root is »prob[ably] of imitative origin«. If he is right, then we may perh. compare Ar ↗ † haǧhaǧa ‘to grumble (camel)’, in which case both [v2] the ‘splitting up in syllables/sounds’ and [v1] the ‘ridiculing, mocking, etc.’ would originally be variations of a camel’s ‘grumbling’, a lion’s ‘growling’ or a pigeon’s ‘cooing’. In a similarly vein, Hoch1994 #377 takes Sem √HGW as »the more common by-form« of √HGː(HGG) (e.g., BiblHbr hāgīg ‘murmuring, whispering’), juxtaposing both Hbr hāgāʰ ‘to growl (animals)’, TargAram hᵃgā (Afʕel) ‘to reason, meditate’, and Ar haǧā ‘to ridicule, disparage’. The author adds that » [t]he semantic development in the various Sem languages is quite varied, but all have to do with mental activities and the uttering of sounds. Hebrew seems to provide the most suitable meanings«. – In this context, we also should consider the fact, observed in DRS 5 (1995) that the root nucleus -HG- alone « a été étoffée de diverses manières dans des racines exprimant des bruits, surtout – mais pas seulement – des sons émis à voix basse, des murmures, etc., par redoublement total (HGHG), par gémination de la troisième radicale (HGG), par adjonction de ʔ final (HGʔ), d’une semi-voyelle (HGW, HGY), d’une liquide (HGL, HGR); on relève aussi, avec des valeurs analogues et la même séquence, des racines à dernière radicale sifflante (HGZ, HGS, HGRS). – Voir aussi sous HGʔ/W/Y. – B. Plusieurs racines, dont certaines des précédentes, comportent la séquence consonantique HG et nomment la notion de *‘sottise, stupidité’, voir ʔHG, HGʔ, HGG, HGHG, HGL, HGʕ, HGRʕ, HWG, HLBG ». ▪ † [v3] : Etymology and relation to the above values obscure, if any. 1 .
